newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's ex-PM Kabariti heads Jordan-Kuwait Bank.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's ex-PM Kabariti heads Jordan-Kuwait Bank.

text.p: Jordan's former Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, architect of Amman's shift away from Iraq, was appointed chairman of Jordan-Kuwait Bank at the behest of members of Kuwait's ruling family, bankers said on Wednesday.

Bankers said Kabariti's appointment on Tuesday was at the recommendation of Kuwaiti Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah, a proponent of restoring full ties with Jordan, damaged after Amman's perceived pro-Iraq sympathy during its seven month occupation of the oil-rich Gulf state in 1990.

"This is in line with the political movements and everyone sees that the economic relationship improves ties more than anything else," former chairman Sufian Sartawi, one of the bank's founders, told Reuters.

Sheikh Sabah and his sons Nasser and Hamad are founders of the bank, owning close to a 50 percent holding through three major investment subsidiaries, Kuwait Investment Projects, Al-Ftouh Investments holding company, and Bahrain-based United Gulf Bank.
During the bank's annual general meeting on Tuesday, the representatives of these firms secured three seats on the seven- member board, along with Kabariti and three other Jordanians.
Kabariti's new post signals his comeback to the public eye since he was sacked as prime minister last March by King Hussein amid differences over handling ties with Israel.

U.S.-educated Kabariti, 47, has a background in finance. He owned a brokerage firm in New York in the 1980s and since leaving the government he set up a new company Strategy Investments Company which provides financial consultancy services and manage investments.
During his 13-month premiership, Kabariti oversaw Jordan's radical shift away from Baghdad after the defection of a leading Iraqi official in 1995.
He lobbied hard for warmer ties with Arab Gulf states and urged Jordanian industrialists to reduce their dependence on the Iraqi market and seek new outlets in the Gulf.

In his new position, bankers expect Kabariti to play a vocal role in encouraging Kuwaiti and Gulf investors back to Jordan, signs of which have already emerged after improved political ties as the Gulf War legacy recedes, coinciding with a more hospitable investment climate.
